scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

Here’s my breakdown of the ethics, psychology, and potential solutions: --- ### **1. Is it "Wrong" to Refuse to Cook? (Ethical Perspective)** **Short answer: It depends on context—but your mom’s reaction suggests a deeper problem.** - **Your side is valid**: - You’re a **high school student** juggling online school, assignments, and likely stress. Expecting you to cook *every night* while also doing homework is unreasonable. - Your mom’s cooking is **inconsistent and low-effort**, and she’s **not holding herself accountable**. If she’s home by 5 PM, she *could* cook—she just chooses not to. - You’re **not the only one** who’s been cooking (your dad has been, and you’ve stepped up before). This isn’t fair. - **But your approach could be improved**: - **Passive refusal ("I won’t cook")** is less effective than **active problem-solving**. Instead of saying, *"Why don’t you cook?"* (which put her on the defensive), try: - *"Mom, I get that you’re home early, but I’m swamped with schoolwork. Can we figure out a schedule where we take turns cooking, or you cook a few nights a week?"* - *"I’ve been cooking a lot lately, but I can’t keep doing it all. Maybe we can split the load?"* - **Avoid guilt-tripping her** ("You’re useless")—it escalates conflict and makes her defensive. Instead, **frame it as a team effort**. - **The bigger issue**: Your mom’s **expectations are unfair**, but her **reaction is toxic**. She’s: - **Shifting blame** ("You’re useless") instead of acknowledging her own role. - **Gaslighting** ("It doesn’t take long to cook")—cooking *well* takes time, especially if she’s not skilled. - **Ignoring the reality** that you’re a student, not a full-time cook. **Verdict on "AITA"?** - **Not wrong** to refuse if you’re overwhelmed, but **your method of refusal was unproductive**. The real issue is **her lack of accountability**—not your cooking. --- ### **2. Why Your Mom Reacts This Way (Psychology)** Her behavior stems from: - **Entitlement**: She’s used to your dad cooking (or her not cooking), so she assumes someone else will always step in. - **Laziness**: She’s **not invested** in learning to cook (despite your dad’s efforts), so she avoids it. - **Shame/Control**: Her outburst ("I’m ashamed of you") suggests she’s **projecting her own insecurities** (e.g., feeling like a failure as a mom) onto you. - **Gender norms**: Many women are **socialized to be the "default" cook**, even when they’re not the best at it. She may not realize how unfair she’s being. --- ### **3. What’s the *Real* Problem?** This isn’t just about dinner—it’s about **fairness, respect, and boundaries**. Your mom is: - **Not pulling her weight** (cooking, chores). - **Demanding more from you** than she does from herself. - **Undermining your dad’s efforts** (he’s the one who *actually* cooks well). - **Creating a cycle of resentment** (you’re tired, she’s frustrated, he’s exhausted). --- ### **4. How to Fix It (Without Burning the House Down)** #### **For You:** ✅ **Set boundaries politely**: - *"Mom, I can’t keep cooking every night with schoolwork. Can we agree on a rotation?"* - *"I’ve been doing most of the cooking—can you help with something else, like setting the table or cleaning up?"* ✅ **Document the unfairness**: - Keep a **list of who does what** (e.g., "Mom: watches TV, Dad: cooks/chores, Me: homework + occasional cooking"). - Show it to your dad—**he’s the only one who can push back against her**. ✅ **Propose solutions**: - **"What if we take turns cooking? I’ll do it tonight, you do it tomorrow."** - **"Can we order takeout once a week so we all have a break?"** - **"Dad, can you help Mom learn to cook a few simple meals?"** (He’s the only one who can change her behavior.) #### **For Your Mom:** 🔹 **Call her out (gently but firmly)**: - *"Mom, I know you’re home early, but cooking takes time. Can we find a way to split it?"* - *"I’ve been cooking a lot—can you help with something else?"* 🔹 **Make her accountable**: - If she refuses to cook, **don’t cook for her**. Eat simple things (pasta, sandwiches) and let her fend for herself. - If she complains, say: *"I’m not cooking for you if you’re not cooking for us."* 🔹 **Get your dad involved**: - He’s the **only one who can change her behavior**. Ask him to: - **Cook more often** (so she sees it’s not just your job). - **Teach her basic meals** (e.g., stir-fry, pasta, soup). - **Set a rule**: *"No one cooks unless it’s their turn."* #### **For Your Dad:** 🔹 **He needs to step up**: - **Cook more** (even if it’s late). - **Teach her** (don’t let her avoid it). - **Talk to her** about fairness: *"We can’t keep relying on you two—let’s share the load."* --- ### **5. Long-Term Fixes** - **Make a family chore chart**: - Assign cooking days, cleaning, etc. **No exceptions**. - **Find a compromise**: - Maybe she cooks **2x a week**, you cook **2x**, and your dad cooks **3x**. - **Therapy or mediation**: - If she’s **emotionally abusive** (shaming, yelling), consider family counseling. --- ### **6. Final Verdict: Was Your Reaction Justified?** **Yes—but your method could’ve been better.** - **You had every right to be annoyed** (you’re doing too much). - **But your mom’s reaction was unfair**, and you could’ve handled it **without escalating the fight**. - **The real issue is her lack of effort**, not your cooking. **What you should do now:** 1. **Calm down** (this isn’t worth the stress). 2. **Talk to your dad**—he’s the only one who can fix this. 3. **Propose a fair system** (cooking rotation, shared chores). 4. **If she refuses, stop cooking for her**—let her see the consequences. --- ### **Score: 0/1?** **0/1**—because while your frustration was **completely justified**, your **method of refusal was unproductive**. The real win is **changing the system**, not just "winning" the argument. **But here’s the kicker:** If your mom **still refuses to change**, then **yes, you’re not wrong for not cooking**—because **she’s not pulling her weight**. The goal isn’t to "win" but to **create a fair, functional household**. Would you like help drafting a message to your dad or mom to start this conversation?
